lessons.title: Spark architecture: driver, executors, cluster manager
lessons.summary: A Spark application is one driver process plus many executor processes.
lessons.remember: The driver plans, the executors do the work one partition per task, and the cluster manager supplies the machines.

lessons.title: SparkSession, SparkContext and running locally
lessons.summary: SparkSession is the single entry point to Spark in modern code.
lessons.remember: SparkSession is the one door into Spark; SparkContext is the older, lower-level door it wraps.

lessons.title: RDD vs DataFrame (and a note on Dataset)
lessons.summary: Spark has three data abstractions: - RDD (Resilient Distributed Dataset): a distributed collection of arbitrary objects.
lessons.remember: In PySpark, use DataFrames; RDDs are a low-level escape hatch and Dataset is a Scala and Java idea.

lessons.title: Lazy evaluation: transformations and actions
lessons.summary: Spark operations come in two kinds: - Transformations (select, filter, join, groupBy, withColumn) return a new DataFrame and only add a step to a plan.
lessons.remember: Transformations build a plan; only actions run it, and every action runs it again unless you cache.

lessons.title: The DAG and RDD lineage
lessons.summary: When an action runs, Spark turns the optimised plan into a DAG (directed acyclic graph) of steps.
lessons.remember: Spark splits the DAG into stages at shuffles, and uses lineage to recompute lost partitions instead of keeping copies.

lessons.title: Schemas and data types
lessons.summary: Every DataFrame has a schema: an ordered list of column names, types and nullability, held as a StructType of StructFields.
lessons.remember: Declare schemas for text sources and use decimals for money; inference is a convenience, not a contract.

lessons.title: Columns, expressions, select and filter
lessons.summary: DataFrame code is built from column expressions.
lessons.remember: A column is an expression, not data; build logic from expressions so Spark can optimise it.

lessons.title: Working with nulls
lessons.summary: Spark SQL follows SQL's null rules: any comparison with null gives null, and a filter keeps only rows where the condition is true.
lessons.remember: Null is "unknown", so comparisons with it are never true; test for it explicitly and use null-safe equality where two unknowns should match.

lessons.title: Sorting, distinct, limit and sampling
lessons.summary: Four everyday operations with very different costs: - orderBy / sort produces a total order across all partitions.
lessons.remember: Global sorts and distincts shuffle everything; ask whether you need them before you write them.

lessons.title: groupBy, aggregation, rollup and cube
lessons.summary: groupBy(keys).agg(...) collapses rows with the same key into one row and computes aggregate expressions: sum, count, avg, min, max, countDistinct, collectlist, first, percentileapprox and many more.
lessons.remember: groupBy shuffles once and aggregates partially first; rollup and cube add subtotal rows marked by grouping().

lessons.title: Joins in Spark
lessons.summary: df.join(other, on, how) combines two DataFrames.
lessons.remember: Join on column names to avoid duplicate keys, use leftsemi and leftanti for existence checks, and watch for key duplication.

lessons.title: Union and set operations
lessons.summary: - union(other) appends rows by position.
lessons.remember: Use unionByName, not union, unless you have checked column order yourself.

lessons.title: Pivot and unpivot
lessons.summary: Pivot turns distinct values of one column into new columns, with an aggregate in each cell: groupBy("product").pivot("month").sum("qty").
lessons.remember: Pivot with an explicit values list; unpivot wide legacy tables into rows early.

lessons.title: Explode and nested data
lessons.summary: JSON, Avro and API data often contain arrays and nested structs.
lessons.remember: explode turns array elements into rows; use explodeouter to keep empty ones and never explode two arrays blindly.

lessons.title: Window functions in Spark
lessons.summary: A window function computes a value for each row from a window of related rows, without collapsing them like groupBy does.
lessons.remember: Windows compute per-row results over related rows; always state the frame when you mean rows, and partition by a key.

lessons.title: Deduplication patterns
lessons.summary: Two kinds of duplicates need two tools: - Exact or key duplicates where any copy will do: dropDuplicates("key") keeps one arbitrary row per key.
lessons.remember: dropDuplicates keeps any copy; when one copy must win, rank with rownumber and a full tie-breaking order.

lessons.title: Built-in functions: string, date, math, conditional
lessons.summary: pyspark.sql.functions (imported as F) holds hundreds of functions that run inside the JVM: - String: upper, trim, concatws, substring, split, regexpreplace, lpad, formatstring.
lessons.remember: Reach for pyspark.sql.functions first; a built-in is almost always faster than anything you write in Python.

lessons.title: Arrays, maps, structs, JSON and regex
lessons.summary: Spark handles nested data natively: - Structs group fields: F.struct(...) builds one, col("a.b") reads one.
lessons.remember: Parse JSON once with a schema, and use higher-order functions to work inside arrays without exploding them.

lessons.title: Python UDFs
lessons.summary: A user-defined function (UDF) runs your own Python function on each row.
lessons.remember: A Python UDF is a black box that ships every row to Python; use it only when no built-in or pandas UDF fits.

lessons.title: pandas UDFs and Apache Arrow
lessons.summary: A pandas UDF (vectorised UDF) receives whole batches of rows as pandas Series or DataFrames instead of one row at a time.
lessons.remember: pandas UDFs move data in Arrow batches, so Python libraries can run on Spark at near-vectorised speed.

lessons.title: Broadcast variables and accumulators
lessons.summary: Two shared-variable tools from the RDD era that still matter: - A broadcast variable sends a read-only value (a lookup dictionary, a small model) to every executor once, instead of with every task.
lessons.remember: Broadcast ships read-only data once per executor; accumulators in transformations can over-count on retries, so do not use them for exact business numbers.

lessons.title: Spark SQL, views, subqueries and CTEs
lessons.summary: Spark SQL and the DataFrame API are two front ends to the same engine.
lessons.remember: SQL and DataFrames compile to the same plan, so pick whichever reads better for each step.

lessons.title: Catalog, databases and tables
lessons.summary: Spark keeps table definitions in a catalog (metastore).
lessons.remember: Managed tables let the catalog own the files; external tables only point at them, and modern catalogs add a third naming level.

lessons.title: Query hints
lessons.summary: Hints tell the optimiser to choose a plan it might not choose itself.
lessons.remember: Hints override the optimiser; use them for proven problems and revisit them when data volumes change.

lessons.title: Reading and writing data, save modes
lessons.summary: spark.read returns a DataFrameReader: you set format, options and an optional schema, then load a path or table.
lessons.remember: Readers set format, options and schema; writers set format and mode, and only a table format makes overwrite safe.

lessons.title: File formats: CSV, JSON, Parquet, ORC, Avro, and compression
lessons.summary: - CSV: text, row-based, no types, many dialects.
lessons.remember: Land raw data in whatever the source gives you, but store analytical data in a columnar format, usually Parquet under a table format.

lessons.title: XML and Excel files
lessons.summary: Legacy systems often hand over XML or spreadsheets.
lessons.remember: XML is readable natively in Spark 4 (via spark-xml before), while Excel is a small-data, driver-side job.

lessons.title: JDBC reads and writes
lessons.summary: Spark reads from and writes to relational databases through JDBC.
lessons.remember: A JDBC read is single-threaded until you give it a partition column or predicates, and every partition is another connection to the source.

lessons.title: Partitioning and bucketing on disk
lessons.summary: Partitioning on disk (df.write.partitionBy("country", "loaddate")) writes one folder per value: .../country=DE/loaddate=2025-10-15/.
lessons.remember: Partition on disk by a low-cardinality filter column such as date; too many partitions is worse than none.

lessons.title: What Microsoft Fabric is
lessons.summary: Microsoft Fabric is a SaaS analytics platform.
lessons.remember: Fabric is one SaaS platform where every workload shares a capacity for compute and OneLake for storage.

lessons.title: OneLake
lessons.summary: OneLake is the single logical data lake that comes with every Fabric tenant.
lessons.remember: OneLake is one ADLS-based lake per tenant, organised by workspace and item, holding Delta tables that every Fabric engine reads.

lessons.title: Tenants, capacities and workspaces
lessons.summary: Fabric has a four-level containment hierarchy: 1.
lessons.remember: Tenant holds settings and OneLake, capacities supply regional compute, workspaces hold items, and domains group workspaces for governance.

lessons.title: Licensing and capacity units
lessons.summary: Fabric is paid mainly through capacities.
lessons.remember: You buy capacity units that every workload shares; bursting and smoothing absorb spikes, and sustained overuse leads to staged throttling.

lessons.title: Fabric vs Synapse, ADF and Power BI Premium
lessons.summary: Fabric is Microsoft's successor platform for several earlier services: - Azure Synapse Analytics: Fabric Data Warehouse, Fabric Spark, pipelines and Eventhouse cover the same ground as dedicated SQL pools, Synapse Spark,
lessons.remember: Fabric absorbs Synapse, ADF and Power BI Premium, but the mapping is not one-to-one and moving is a project, not a switch.

lessons.title: Lakehouse
lessons.summary: A Lakehouse is a Fabric item that stores data in OneLake and is designed to be written mainly by Spark (notebooks, Spark job definitions) and by Data Factory.
lessons.remember: A Lakehouse is Spark-first storage with a Files area for anything and a Tables area of Delta tables that every Fabric engine can read.

lessons.title: Warehouse
lessons.summary: A Fabric Warehouse is a relational data warehouse you build and load with T-SQL.
lessons.remember: The Warehouse is the T-SQL-first, read-write store in Fabric, with multi-table transactions and Delta storage underneath.

lessons.title: SQL analytics endpoint
lessons.summary: The SQL analytics endpoint is a read-only T-SQL interface that Fabric creates automatically for each lakehouse, mirrored database and SQL database (exactly one per item).
lessons.remember: The SQL analytics endpoint gives read-only T-SQL over lakehouse tables, with a sync delay and with security that protects only the SQL path.

lessons.title: Shortcuts
lessons.summary: A shortcut is a pointer in OneLake to data stored somewhere else.
lessons.remember: A shortcut is a zero-copy pointer to data elsewhere; external shortcuts read with a shared delegated credential.

lessons.title: Mirroring
lessons.summary: Mirroring continuously replicates data from an operational or analytical source into OneLake as Delta tables, without you building pipelines.
lessons.remember: Mirroring is managed, near real-time replication of a source into read-only Delta tables in OneLake, with free replication compute.

lessons.title: Delta format in Fabric
lessons.summary: Delta Lake is Fabric's common table format.
lessons.remember: Everything in Fabric is Delta in OneLake; V-Order and regular compaction decide how fast it reads.

lessons.title: Data Factory pipelines
lessons.summary: A Fabric pipeline orchestrates work: it runs activities in order, with branching, loops, parameters and error paths.
lessons.remember: Fabric pipelines are ADF's orchestration model inside Fabric, minus datasets and SSIS, plus native Fabric activities.

lessons.title: Dataflows Gen2
lessons.summary: Dataflow Gen2 is low-code data preparation with Power Query, the same engine used in Excel and Power BI.
lessons.remember: Dataflow Gen2 is Power Query in Fabric: great for low-code shaping at moderate volume, costly for heavy lifting.

lessons.title: Copy job
lessons.summary: A Copy job is a Fabric item that moves data from a source to a destination without building a pipeline.
lessons.remember: Copy job is managed bulk and incremental copy with built-in state, the simplest way to land source tables in Fabric.

lessons.title: On-premises and VNet data gateways
lessons.summary: Fabric is a cloud service, so it needs a bridge to reach data behind a firewall: - The on-premises data gateway is Windows software you install on a machine inside your network.
lessons.remember: Use the on-premises gateway for data inside your own network and the VNet gateway for private Azure sources; Spark and Direct Lake do not go through gateways.

lessons.title: Batch, CDC and streaming ingestion (sample)
lessons.summary: There are three common ways to move data from source systems into an analytics platform: periodic batch copies, change data capture (CDC), and event streaming.
lessons.remember: Batch copies snapshots, CDC copies changes, streaming copies events.
